name: Back extension / deadlift strength
lead: Deadlifts and back extensions are posterior-chain exercises that build the muscles running down the back of the body: the glutes, hamstrings and the erector spinae along the spine, with the lats and traps also working in the deadlift.[1][2] Lifters use them to develop a thicker, more muscular back and hips, and many pair them with posture goals, aiming for a stronger, more upright frame.

The deadlift lifts a weight from the floor to hip level and lowers it again, most often with a barbell; it is one of the three powerlifting lifts and a strongman event.[1] The back extension, also called hyperextension, strengthens the erector spinae by arching the spine back from a bent-forward position on a Roman chair, a 45-degree bench or a reverse-hyperextension machine, or with no equipment.[2]

Encyclopedic sources describe the muscles worked, the variations and the technique points, while research on back-extensor strength mostly concerns back-muscle endurance tests, torque production and rehabilitation rather than appearance.[2][4][5] Posture itself is linked in psychology research to how confident and open a person looks to others.[6]

angle.text: These lifts add muscle to the back of the body, which shows up as a fuller back, glutes and hamstrings. Lifters also use them to build the trunk strength they associate with standing and sitting tall.

paras: The conventional deadlift is described as working the gluteus maximus most, with the quadriceps, hamstrings, trapezius, latissimus dorsi and erector spinae also involved; the lumbar muscles contract isometrically to stabilise the spine during setup.[1] Variations include sumo, rack pulls, deficit, single-leg, trap-bar and stiff-leg deadlifts, and the Romanian deadlift, which is associated with posterior-chain development and was popularised by Romanian weightlifters.[1][3]
For looks, the appeal is that one lift loads most of the back of the body at once, which proponents link to back thickness, glute and hamstring development and a stronger-looking trunk.

The back extension works the erector spinae. In the 90-degree Roman chair version the body lies horizontally for full range of motion, while the 45-degree bench gives a shorter range. The reverse hyperextension machine is described as also working the glutes and part of the hamstrings, and a 2019 biomechanical study in the Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research reportedly compared it with the standard hyperextension and found greater hip range of motion.[2]

Back-extensor strength is measured in research with isometric endurance tests such as the Sorensen test, and a literature review found six types of such tests, with motivation and effort of the subject as limiting factors.[4] A study of lumbar back-extensor mechanics examined how torque is produced about the lumbar spine.[7]

Common deadlift errors listed include protracting the shoulders, letting the bar drift from the body, rounding the back and turning the lift into a squat. The article says whether back rounding is harmful is controversial and that excessive rounding may lead to injury, and describes the trap-bar variant as generally less taxing on the lower back.[1] For back extensions, the only explicit guidance in the encyclopedia article is to start with lighter weights to avoid straining the back muscles.[2]

On the T Nation forum, back extensions, good mornings, reverse hypers and deadlifts appear together in posted programmes aimed at the lower back and posterior chain, and members list stiff-legged deadlifts, Romanian deadlifts, hip thrusts and back extensions among their staple lifts.[8][9]

No studies found testing deadlifts or back extensions as an intervention for appearance or posture. Related research includes a review of isometric back-extension endurance tests, a randomised comparison of integrated versus isolated core exercises using muscle activation in the erector spinae, rectus abdominis and obliques, and a systematic review of physical functioning measures as predictors in low back pain.[4][5][10]

lore.intro: In strength and looksmaxxing circles, deadlifts and back extensions are discussed as the core of posterior-chain training, mentioned alongside rows, good mornings and hip thrusts in programmes shared on T Nation.[8][9]

quick.overview:
The deadlift lifts a weight from the floor to hip level and is one of the three powerlifting lifts. The back extension is a bodyweight or weighted exercise that works the erector spinae muscles along the spine. Both are used in strength training to build the muscles of the back of the body.

In posture and looksmaxxing discussions they are framed as ways to build a stronger back and hips. Wikipedia describes the mechanics and muscles involved but not research on posture or appearance, and no trial found tests either exercise for those outcomes.
quick.mechanism: The conventional deadlift mainly works the glutes, with the quadriceps, hamstrings, trapezius, lats and erector spinae contributing. Back extensions target the erector spinae (spinalis, longissimus, iliocostalis) and, in reverse-hyperextension machines, the glutes and part of the hamstrings.
quick.risks: Wikipedia lists rounding the back as a common error, calling it controversial and saying excessive rounding may lead to injury. Trap-bar versions are described as generally less taxing on the lower back. Back extension guidance on the same source advises lighter loads for beginners to avoid straining the back.
